Lecture 23

Fourier representation, inversion and standard pairs

Lecture objectives

We fix the Fourier convention, prove the inversion formula for continuous integrable functions with integrable transforms by Gaussian regularization, and prove a symmetric-cutoff inversion theorem that returns the half-sum at a jump. We derive the standard pairs, introduce cosine and sine transforms, and collect conventions and pairs on one card.

GM 35 wrote a periodic function as a Fourier series, a sum of oscillations whose frequencies are the multiples of one fundamental frequency. A pulse, a decaying signal or a wave packet on the whole line has no period. In this lecture we represent such a function by an integral over a continuum of wave numbers, its Fourier transform. We use the nascent deltas and the standing rules for improper integrals of Lecture 22 as tools. The representation is a theorem with hypotheses, not a definition. Along the way we compute the standard pairs: the rectangular pulse with the sine integral of Lecture 20, the Gaussian with the complex Gaussian integral of Lecture 18, and the two-sided and one-sided exponentials with the residues of Lecture 19. The lecture reads in three stages: the convention and the pairs (Sections 23.1–23.3), inversion (Sections 23.4–23.5), and half-line transforms with the card (Sections 23.6–23.7).

23.1 From Fourier series to the Fourier transform

We first fix the class of functions.

Definition 23.1 (Piecewise continuous, piecewise C1,C^1C1, integrable). A function f:R→Cf:\R\to\Cf:R→C is piecewise continuous (Lecture 22, in an equivalent form) if every bounded interval [α,β][\alpha,\beta][α,β] has a finite partition such that on each open piece fff has a continuous extension to the closed piece. It is piecewise C1C^1C1 if moreover on each open piece fff is differentiable and f′f'f′ has a continuous extension to the closed piece. A piecewise continuous fff is integrable on R\RR if ∫−∞∞∣f(x)∣ ⁣dx<∞.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\abs{f(x)}\dd x<\infty .∫−∞∞​∣f(x)∣dx<∞.

A complex-valued function is continuous, or integrable, when its real and imaginary parts are, and its integral is the integral of the real part plus i\iui times that of the imaginary part (GM 35). The piecewise C1C^1C1 functions are those of GM 35, without periodicity. The values at the partition points do not affect integrals, and at every point xxx the one-sided limits f(x−)f(x^-)f(x−) and f(x+)f(x^+)f(x+) exist. Lecture 22’s rules I1–I3 apply to this class. It is narrower than the locally integrable functions of Lecture 22: ∣x∣−1/2e−x2\abs x^{-1/2}\ee^{-x^2}∣x∣−1/2e−x2 is locally integrable, but not piecewise continuous on R.\RR.

For a period 2L2L2L the complex Fourier coefficients of GM 35, transferred from the period 2π2\pi2π by the substitution x=Ly/π,x=Ly/\pix=Ly/π, are cn=12L∫−LLf(x)e−iknx ⁣dx,kn=nπL(n∈Z),c_n=\frac1{2L}\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\ee^{-\iu k_nx}\dd x,\qquad k_n=\frac{n\pi}L\quad(n\in\Z),cn​=2L1​∫−LL​f(x)e−ikn​xdx,kn​=Lnπ​(n∈Z), and the series reads ∑n∈Zcneiknx.\sum_{n\in\Z}c_n\ee^{\iu k_nx}∑n∈Z​cn​eikn​x. The wave numbers knk_nkn​ have the spacing Δk=π/L.\Delta k=\pi/LΔk=π/L. With f^L(k)=(2π)−1/2∫−LLf(x)e−ikx ⁣dx\widehat f_L(k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\ee^{-\iu kx}\dd xf​L​(k)=(2π)−1/2∫−LL​f(x)e−ikxdx we have cn=(2π)−1/2f^L(kn)Δk,c_n=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\widehat f_L(k_n)\Delta kcn​=(2π)−1/2f​L​(kn​)Δk, so that ∑n∈Zcneiknx=12π∑n∈Zf^L(kn)eiknxΔk.\sum_{n\in\Z}c_n\ee^{\iu k_nx}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{n\in\Z}\widehat f_L(k_n)\ee^{\iu k_nx}\Delta k .n∈Z∑​cn​eikn​x=2π​1​n∈Z∑​f​L​(kn​)eikn​xΔk. The right side looks like a Riemann sum, and as L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞ it suggests the pair of formulas below. This is a heuristic, not a proof: two limits are taken at once over an unbounded range. Definition 23.2 (Fourier transform). For fff integrable on R\RR the Fourier transform of fff is the function f^=F ⁣[f]:R→C\widehat f=\FT{f}:\R\to\Cf​=F[f]:R→C given by f^(k)=F ⁣[f](k)=12π∫−∞∞e−ikxf(x) ⁣dx.\widehat f(k)=\FT{f}(k)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd x .f​(k)=F[f](k)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​e−ikxf(x)dx.(23.1) For a function ggg of kkk the inverse transform is F−1 ⁣[g](x)=12π∫−∞∞eikxg(k) ⁣dk,\IFT{g}(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}g(k)\dd k ,F−1[g](x)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxg(k)dk,(23.2) whenever the integral converges in a stated sense.

The variable kkk is the wave number. The forward transform carries e−ikx,\ee^{-\iu kx}e−ikx, the inverse carries e+ikx,\ee^{+\iu kx}e+ikx, and each carries the factor (2π)−1/2.(2\pi)^{-1/2}(2π)−1/2. For a signal f(t)f(t)f(t) in time we use the same formulas with ttt for xxx and the angular frequency ω\omegaω for k,kk, with the same signs. The integral (23.1) converges absolutely, because ∣e−ikxf(x)∣=∣f(x)∣.\abs{\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)}=\abs{f(x)}​e−ikxf(x)​=∣f(x)∣. Whether the inverse integral (23.2) converges, and whether it returns f,ff, is the subject of this lecture. The function f^\widehat ff​ is also called the spectrum of f.ff.

A Fourier series uses the discrete wave numbers knk_nkn​ of a periodic function; a Fourier transform uses a continuum of wave numbers for a function on the whole line. The two are different objects with different normalizations.

Exchanges of limits and integrals below use Lecture 22’s rule I1 (dominated limits, with the parameter form I1(b)) and rule I3 (Fubini–Tonelli); each use names the rule.

23.4 Inversion on a smooth class

The spectrum of the pulse is not integrable, while the Gaussian spectrum decays faster than every power of 1/∣k∣.1/\abs k1/∣k∣. For functions whose spectrum is integrable the inverse integral converges absolutely, and it returns the function.

Theorem 23.6 (Fourier inversion). Let fff be continuous and integrable on R,\RR, and let f^\widehat ff​ be integrable on R.\RR. Then for every x∈Rx\in\Rx∈R f(x)=12π∫−∞∞eikxf^(k) ⁣dk,f(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f(k)\dd k ,f(x)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxf​(k)dk,(23.9) the integral converging absolutely. In other notation, F−1 ⁣[F ⁣[f]]=f.\IFT{\FT f}=fF−1[F[f]]=f.

Proof. We insert the Gaussian factor e−εk2/2\ee^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}e−εk2/2 into the inverse integral, exchange the order of integration, and let ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+ on both sides. Fix x∈R.x\in\Rx∈R. For ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 put Iε=12π∫−∞∞eikxe−εk2/2f^(k) ⁣dk.I_\varepsilon=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}\ee^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}\widehat f(k)\dd k .Iε​=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxe−εk2/2f​(k)dk.

Step 1: the left side. For each kkk the integrand tends to eikxf^(k)\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f(k)eikxf​(k) as ε→0+,\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+, and its modulus is at most ∣f^(k)∣,\abs{\widehat f(k)}​f​(k)​, which is integrable by hypothesis. By rule I1, IεI_\varepsilonIε​ tends to the right side of (23.9).

Step 2: the exchange. 23.5 Piecewise C1C^1C1 functions and jumps

The pulse is not continuous, and its spectrum is not integrable. Example 23.4 nevertheless found the limit of the symmetric-cutoff inverse at every point. The same holds for every integrable piecewise C1C^1C1 function. The proof needs one lemma on oscillating integrals.

The pulse is an instance of Theorem 23.9, with the one-sided limits 111 and 000 at x=a;x=ax=a; the theorem does not require f^\widehat ff​ to be integrable.

Theorem 23.9 recovers values at jumps only through a convention. Changing fff at finitely many points does not change f^,\widehat ff​, so no inversion formula can recover the value that fff was given at a jump; the symmetric cutoff returns the half-sum. Lecture 25 compares functions and spectra through integrals of squared moduli, which do not see values at finitely many points; such statements differ in kind from the pointwise statement (23.10).

23.6 Cosine and sine transforms

Parity simplifies the transform. If fff is integrable and even, then e−ikx=cos⁡(kx)−isin⁡(kx),\ee^{-\iu kx}=\cos(kx)-\iu\sin(kx)e−ikx=cos(kx)−isin(kx), the term with sin⁡(kx)f(x)\sin(kx)f(x)sin(kx)f(x) is odd in xxx and integrates to zero, and f^(k)=2π∫0∞f(x)cos⁡(kx) ⁣dx,\widehat f(k)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(kx)\dd x ,f​(k)=π2​​∫0∞​f(x)cos(kx)dx, which is even in k.kk. If fff is odd, the cosine term integrates to zero, and f^(k)=−i2π∫0∞f(x)sin⁡(kx) ⁣dx,\widehat f(k)=-\iu\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(kx)\dd x ,f​(k)=−iπ2​​∫0∞​f(x)sin(kx)dx, which is odd in k.kk. A function given only on the half-line (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) can be extended to an even or to an odd function on R,\RR, and the two formulas above become transforms on the half-line.

Amplitude, phase and spectral lines. The spectrum describes a function by the amplitude ∣f^(k)∣\abs{\widehat f(k)}​f​(k)​ and the phase arg⁡f^(k)\arg\widehat f(k)argf​(k) of each wave number. Summary

The Fourier transform f^(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf(x) ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd xf​(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf(x)dx of an integrable function is bounded and continuous and tends to zero at infinity. Gaussian regularization and rule I3 prove inversion when the transform is integrable; the sine integral of Lecture 20 and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma prove the symmetric-cutoff inversion with half-sums at jumps. The pulse spectrum, a rescaled sin⁡k/k,\sin k/ksink/k, is not integrable. The widths of the pulse and Gaussian spectra are reciprocal to the widths of the functions.

  • Convention: f^(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{-\iu kx}f\dd xf​(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxfdx and f(x)=(2π)−1/2∫eikxf^ ⁣dk;f(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f\dd kf(x)=(2π)−1/2∫eikxf​dk; the same with ttt and ω;\omegaω; conversions on the card.

  • Inversion: if fff is continuous and integrable and f^\widehat ff​ is integrable, the inverse integral converges absolutely to f(x)f(x)f(x) at every x;xx; this holds for f∈S(R).f\in\Schwartz(\R)f∈S(R).

  • Jumps: if fff is integrable and piecewise C1,C^1C1, lim⁡R→∞(2π)−1/2∫−RReikxf^ ⁣dk=12(f(x+)+f(x−));\lim_{R\to\infty}(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-R}^{R}\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f\dd k=\tfrac12(f(x^+)+f(x^-))limR→∞​(2π)−1/2∫−RR​eikxf​dk=21​(f(x+)+f(x−)); values at jumps are recovered only through this convention.

  • Pairs: Πa^=2/πsin⁡(ka)/k;\widehat{\Pi_a}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\sin(ka)/kΠa​​=2/π​sin(ka)/k; F ⁣[e−x2/(2σ2)]=σe−σ2k2/2;\FT{\ee^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}}=\sigma\ee^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}F[e−x2/(2σ2)]=σe−σ2k2/2; F ⁣[e−a∣x∣]=2/π a/(a2+k2);\FT{\ee^{-a\abs x}}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,a/(a^2+k^2)F[e−a∣x∣]=2/π​a/(a2+k2); the transform of an even function is the cosine transform of its restriction to (0,∞),(0,\infty)(0,∞), and that of an odd function is −i-\iu−i times the sine transform.

Lecture 24 derives the operational rules of the transform and extends it to tempered distributions, such as constants, sinusoids and the delta.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. A dimensionless pulse is f(x)=3f(x)=3f(x)=3 for ∣x∣<1\abs x<1∣x∣<1 and zero for ∣x∣>1\abs x>1∣x∣>1. In the course’s unitary Fourier convention, find f^(0)\widehat f(0)f​(0). Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. At zero wave number the exponential factor is constant. Keep the forward normalization.

At k=0k=0k=0 the exponential factor is one. The pulse has integral 3⋅2=63\cdot2=63⋅2=6. Multiplying by the forward factor 1/2π1/\sqrt{2\pi}1/2π​ gives f^(0)=6/2π\widehat f(0)=6/\sqrt{2\pi}f​(0)=6/2π​. Omitting the factor would give the answer in an unnormalized forward convention.

2. For the unit-height rectangular pulse on (−a,a)(-a,a)(−a,a) with a>0a>0a>0, which statement describes the Fourier inverse given by the lecture’s inversion theorems?

Hint. Compare the absolute inverse integrand with the modulus of the spectrum, which is proportional to sin⁡(ak)/k\sin(ak)/ksin(ak)/k.

The pulse spectrum is proportional to sin⁡(ak)/k\sin(ak)/ksin(ak)/k. Its modulus has a divergent integral, since on fixed-length pieces of successive periods the sine stays bounded away from zero and the resulting lower bounds form a harmonic sum. The inverse phase on the real line has modulus one for every evaluation point. Thus compact support in the original variable and evaluating away from the jumps do not give absolute convergence. The pulse is piecewise C1C^1C1, so symmetric-cutoff inversion still gives the half-sum of the one-sided limits, including at a jump.

3. Let an integrable piecewise C1C^1C1 function have left limit 555 and right limit 111 at zero, where its assigned value is 000. What does the symmetric-cutoff Fourier inverse give at zero?

Hint. The inversion theorem uses one-sided limits. Check whether a value assigned at a single point affects the transform.

The theorem gives (5+1)/2=3(5+1)/2=3(5+1)/2=3. Either one-sided limit by itself loses the contribution from the other side. The assigned value 000 changes the function at one point only and leaves its Fourier transform unchanged.

4. A unit-height rectangular pulse equals one for −a<x<a-a<x<a−a<x<a and zero outside [−a,a][-a,a][−a,a], with a>0a>0a>0. Measure its spectral main-lobe width in wave number kkk, from the first negative zero to the first positive zero. What is that width?

Hint. Find the first nonzero roots of sin⁡(ak)=0\sin(ak)=0sin(ak)=0. The value at the origin is found by a limit.

The spectrum is proportional to sin⁡(ak)/k\sin(ak)/ksin(ak)/k, with nonzero limit at zero. Its first zeros are k=±π/ak=\pm\pi/ak=±π/a, so their separation is 2π/a2\pi/a2π/a. The value π/a\pi/aπ/a is the distance to a single zero. A value of π/(2a)\pi/(2a)π/(2a) uses the full pulse width in the sine argument where the half-width belongs, then measures only to that zero. The value 4π/a4\pi/a4π/a uses the second pair of zeros.
